datasetName: Sea Watch Foundation Marine Megafauna Sightings: 1971 to present
fieldNotes: I first spotted the Orcas from the high road that overlooks the harbour in Collieston at 13.05 when I saw a blow with my naked eye. With my binoculars I then saw the distinctive tall fins of Killer Whales. I attracted the attention of some of the villagers who help put out the news by phone and Facebook. and before very long  many residents had got views of the animals that initially may have been as little as 2 km out. but very gradually drifted north and much further out. The pod. which our best estimate at about 14.15 was of 8 whales. was visible from Cransdale Head up to 16.00. all the time very active and sometimes probably feeding. The next significant village north. Whinnyfold. had observers getting better views by this time. A count was made there of 15 animals. but I would be a bit cautious without knowing their evidence for this. Villagers believe this is the first definite sighting in Collieston for about 15 years.

fieldNotes: It was 1996 I am in the summer we were fishing two of us preparing for night fishing of Sound bank on the Edge south of the river Erme in Devon it must be about an hour before Dusk me and my friend early were preparing to start whats a bottom and on the other side of the river from us about maybe 100m fin deeper side of the river going quite slow we must have seen it for about quarter to 20 minutes before it went up around the Headland and out towards the sea but we did have activity earlier on in with sealine skulls of fish up the river the thing but I have only just recognised through visiting their National  Aquarium in Plymouth and people were talking about a sighting in same place couple of months ago alarm syncing this John Finn what looks like an orca thing we thought it was a basking shark looking at a basking shark it is a lot wider this was tall and dark and it was menacing I always thought about that that day I was trying to work out what it was because I honestly didnt think they came into our region didnt think it was like used to say we used to fish every weekend for the summer look quite a few years I am pissed in a while but I was remember that day because it is probably the strangest thing that ever happened cummings no fish that live in the river islands quite a boring night. fieldNotes: I was travelling on the ferry for annual leave. I am employed as an ecologist submit records and consider myself a credible witness. This is the first time I have seen a Killer Whale.I was on deck bird watching when I noticed the whale porpoising and spouting in the distance coming towards us. The boat was travelling fast as was the whale in the opposite direction intermittently porpoising with fin in full view. with saddle also visible and blowing spray it was very impressive. I had binoculars. but even my wife without binoculars could appreciate what species this was. We were able to watch as the whale passed and into the distance probably for 5 mins.I am sure that this was a male Killer Whale and appeared to be on it's own.My wife Rachel Gray and another lady passenger also witnessed the event.

fieldNotes: Seen to be tail splashing and leaping partially out of water. just west of Eileen Dearg in loch Riddon. Circling in same area clockwise several times for approximately 10 minutes. So exciting! Awesome to see.

datasetName: Sea Watch Foundation Marine Megafauna Sightings: 1971 to present
fieldNotes: The day that most of Shetland saw the Killer Whales!  They made their way slowly up the east coast from Sumburgh to Lerwick. then around Bressay to Noss.  All the way up the coast they were observed hunting Common Seals. Eiders and fish. and appeared to comprise of at least 3 family groups. with 3 large males. a juvenile and a calf.  Our encounter involved several females hunting seals in a small bay in Gulberwick where I was lucky enough to catch them killing a seal on video. which can be seen on the Shetland Orca Sightings group.

fieldNotes: Sighting from fishery protection vessel 'Hirta'. Wind NNE 13 kts. Barometer 1011.6. Air temp 8.0'C. Sea Temp 4.5'C. The calf tail-slapped twice during the time and one very obvious male with the pod.  There was a group of gannets. common and herring gulls in the same area(Maybe 100 birds). Apart from the fishing boat the were no other vessels in the area.  The Captain took 2 or 3 photos of individuals which we could forward on to you.  Hope this information is of some help.

fieldNotes: A Night to Remember North of Mousa Sound(footage and photographs available through the Shetland Orca Sightings Facebook group)Killer WhalesMousa Sound. north31st July 2016. 20:30 ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â‚¬Å“ 22:00Sea state: Rough (6)Swell Height: ModerateWind Direction: NWVisibility: 1-5kmObservers:  Craig Nisbet. Melvin Redeker. Fiona Van Doorn07734 837417Noss NNRBressayShetlandSo there I was. running the Noss ferry like it was any other day when I saw my mates Melvin and Fiona blazing into view in their shiny new RIB.  Freshly arrived from the annual migration north from the Netherlands and barely settled in Nesting. theyÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢d already been out scouting Yell Sound in search of our giant pied friends.  With little success up north. they set off to Noss for a wee visit. and who knew how this particular day would pan out!Visitors were first on the case. with Shetlander Steve Hawick picking up a pod of approximately 5 individuals including a calf 100m below the spectacular viewpoint over to the Noup of Noss.  Steve wasnÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢t the only visitor lucky enough to get these unrivalled aerial views- our friend and regular visitor Hannah Bateson was also over for a visit with her pals and they were. as they say. in the right place at the right time.  Spanish visitor Marta was also over at the time and managed some cracking shots of mother and calf from above.  Of course. one of the boat trips around the island was bound to get lucky. and today it was the turn of Shetland Seabird Tours. who appeared to have the pod right alongside them for some time.  Both wardens were unable to share the experience. as the pod had moved south east by the time word got back to Andy. who made every effort to relocate them and return to Noss Sound in quick time to share the news.  The excitement waned with the realisation that the pod had passed us by. and we could only take satisfaction in the joy of a dozen or so visitors that had memorable views from the cliffs.  So it was back to the plan as we prepared to set out to monitor the Bonxie plot that evening.  That was until the rain set in!At this stage Fiona was in for a cup of tea. and Melvin was returning from what he described as a very enjoyable dive at the GiantÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢s Leg on the south side of Bressay.   With the visitors off. Melvin offered to take me out for a wee ride in the new boat.  Now this was a step up from last yearÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢s Zodiac. and a beast of a machine when it came to cutting through otherwise fearsome swell.  Conditions would have been unpleasant to say the least for the Noss ferry in this water. but a trip around the Noup on this particular evening in this vessel was as simple as cruise control.The Noup. Kittiwakes. Bonxies going for Gannets. the ugliest chick in the colony and the search for the last of the jumplings. before Melvin decides he fancies a speculative look out to sea.  MelvinÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢s seen the big fish before. and is aware of how quickly they can move. and of their occasional tendency to linger in deeper water.  For me I was just keen to see Noss from a new angle!A rice cake each. and a quick check on Shetland Orca Sightings (4G is readily available in the inshore waters on the east side of Shetland with EE folks!) presented us with a decision: do we head to Fladdabister . or return to Noss and part company for the evening?  News of Killer Whales no more than a 30 minute run from our current location left us with little choice.  Beyond Bressay the RIB (call sign Orca) cut her way through ever strengthening swell from the North West until she neared the eastern coast of mainland Shetland. nearby where the pod had been reported not half an hour previously.  It was at this point that a couple of saving graces came into play: a comment from Gina Scanlon on Facebook referred to their current location as nearby orange RIB!  At this we began to feel extreme frustration.  Where were they?!  While we scanned the sea in vain. the phone rang: it was Hugh Harrop.  Having been contacted by Gina. Hugh called me and recommended that we head toward Mousa Sound as thatÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢s where he was on route to from Lerwick.  So with eyes peeled we proceeded south along the coast toward Mousa with hopes now high.  We turned the corner around Helliness and into the bay to the north of Mousa Sound.  A dark wall of rain loomed over the mainland. and there in front of us appeared a pod of Killer Whales!  Initially only brief views. they appeared to be swimming south. so we tried to keep our distance and maintain a steady pace. aware that if they chose to. they could be away from us in seconds.  I was contacted by Hugh again who was now onto them from the roadside near Sandwick. and he told us they were behind us.  We soon relocated them. and by giving them a wide berth and killing the engine and sonar to the north west. we were able to drift toward them at close range as they apparently fed. rolling on the surface into repeated shallow dives.  During three drifts into the pod we observed at least five females. one of which has been identified as 019 (ÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã‹Å“MousaÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢). a large male and at least one calf. presumably one of last yearÃƒÂ¢Ã¢â€šÂ¬Ã¢â€žÂ¢s.  As well as diving to catch fish. other forms of behaviour included logging both from the females and the male. a full breach from one female. partial breaching from the youngster and repeated spy-hopping close into the boat. possibly to investigate what the splashing was from the side of the boat.  As the light faded it became impossible for our already inadequate camera and two GoPros to record any more footage or photographs. and we were left for a further 10 minutes or so drifting in Mousa Sound with a pod of apex predators in awe of their size. strength and beauty. positively buzzing from the experience. cold in the choppy. windy and wet conditions and nevertheless reluctant to head back to Noss and call it a night.

datasetName: Sea Watch Foundation Marine Megafauna Sightings: 1971 to present
fieldNotes: An incredible encounter. Photographs are being looked at currently to determine the number of individuals but it may take some time with other work priorities. The estimate of 10+ may rise when we analyse the pictures. it appears there were some animals from the morning pod seen later in the evening. Two animals were seen at 0520 hrs. then at 0700 hrs a pod of six including at least 2 Bulls (no calves) were hunting seals around the island for several hours. They were not observed to definitely kill any seals but at several points they had Seals at their mercy but did not finish them off. Then at 1845 hrs a pod of at least 10 individuals were seen from the dining room table and were seen to contain 2 calves. They then preceded to circle the island and came in to the North Haven where they cornered a Grey Seal. The surrounded it and showed aggression towards it but didnt kill it. All kinds of behaviour were observed as they swam right below us. one of the calves was tail slapping regularly. they were heard calling to each other. swimming in reverse and tail fluking. Eventually at 1955 the noise of the approaching Good Shepherd ferry seemed to disturb them. They headed at speed south around Buness and then after hunting in the bays for a while disappeared south around Sheep Rock at around 2030 hrs. There are many pictures on the Fair Isle Bird Obs Facebook page and a video of them with the seal on the Fair Isle Bird Obs youtube channel. We will try and ascertain the number of individuals and Ill send the details on an email. Some people have suggested online that the pod contained animals previously recognized. HuLK 62. Nott. scottish ID No.18 and IS229/SN067. Please get in touch if you require any more information.

fieldNotes: 3 magical encounters of the  2 males  John Coe  and Aquarius today . Each encounter we spent approx 10 mins in "their" area, keeping at least 130m & low engine revs.; 1st encounter as submitted here.; 2nd at approx 14.35 approx 3 miles S of Blasket sound ( between Slea Head & Blasket Mor); Final encounter at approx  15.50 just NE of Black Sound ( between Blasket Mor and Inishnabro). ; JC and Aquarius travelling swiftly & stealthily in general W to S W direction.; Unfortunately disturbance by fast rib getting too close during last encounter caused JC and Aquarius to dive & as we left area they were not seen resurfacing again, despite constant scanning through binoculars,  for 15 plus mins. ; A dream finally come true after many years searching for these 2 amazing surviving creatures ,working on eco & scientific boats in Scotland & Ireland . Truely amazing!!!!; With Blasket Islands Eco Marine tours ;

datasetName: Sea Watch Foundation Marine Megafauna Sightings: 1971 to present
fieldNotes: David Clark and I were at Porth Ysgaden near Tudweiliog on the Lleyn peninsular on 5/10/16 at roughly 13.00 pm. We both saw one large whale with a very obvious pointed dorsal fin followed by two small groups with around 3 individuals in each which kept surfacing. we both saw clear black and white markings and I saw clearly a black and white head coming out of the water.  David very clearly saw a smaller individual in the group jumping. which he presumed was a juvenile.  We have both seen bottlenose dolphins. porpoise and other species of large marine mammals frequently in the past and are quite certain of our identification.  We watched them for around 30 minutes.

fieldNotes: Orca reported Scapa Flow near Hoy and Houton by Helen Hadley this being the second sighting in 2 days. Karen Munro set of for the East coast hopping they would cross the Pentland Firth and follow the tide South. Karen spotted a group of Killer Whales 1 mile off Aukengill Harbour car park. I went North and met Dan Brown who was watching the group that were about 1 mile off shore going South. ( karen had returned home) Dan and myself watched them pass Kiess Harbour. I remained at Kiess to ensure they did not change direction while Dan rushed to Noss Head. When I saw they were going to pass the Headland I headed for Wick. on the way Dan confirmed they were rounding the headland and heading South towards Wick at 8pm.. When I got to Trinkie on the South side of the Wick river there were about a dozen cars and dozens of people who had been alerted by the web page. I up dated some of them and after 20 mins the Orca came into view about 100 to 150 meters from the shore and moved very slowly South. I estimated their average speed from time and distanced covered they were moving at 2 mph.There were a lot of very happy people who got to see them pass by. many seeing Orca for the first time.One of the females was identified Icelandic KW Mousa Scottish catalogue 019.See attached Pictures sighting entered on line (Karen Munro)

fieldNotes: My crew Sue & I saw one Orca dorsal fin 3 times: it surfaced once on the port side, then on the starboard side and again on the port side. I put the engine in neutral so the propeller would not harm it.  Just under the surface I could see it's large round black head and Sue said she definitely saw white patches under the water. Afterwards we checked lots of identification guides but the only match was an Orca. I reported it to Ilfracombe Harbourmaster. He wondered if we'd seen a Rissos dolphin - I'm sure it wasn't- I've seen them several times in Welsh waters.
